newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr stalls at the upside hurdle.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr stalls at the upside hurdle.

text.p: An afternoon burst of samurai related buying proved insufficient to push the Australian dollar back above minor resistance at US$0.7900, leaving the dollar trapped in a 30 point range.

With selling kicking in on any signs of an uptick, and buyers having established support below US$0.7870, there was little to drive the dollar, especially in the absence of any major local data in the next week or so, traders said.
By 4.45 p.m. (0645 GMT), the Australian dollar was at US$0.7890/95 from an early US0.7885/90 and US$0.7884/89 late on Wednesday. On the day, the unit traded a US$0.7871/98 range.
The samurai rumours were proved correct when the NSW Treasury Corporation announced the launch of a 20 billion yen three year Aussie/yen dual currency bond late in the day.
Sentiment had favoured a downside test this morning, but the buying interest below US$0.7870 surprised some of the bears, and then the samurai interest added to the unit's strength.
Traders said there appeared to be some sell orders above US$0.7900, but the volume here was limited and the US$0.7910/20 resistance area was the real test for the Australian dollar.
The recent star performer of the region, the New Zealand dollar, drifted lower through the day, trading under US$0.7000.

The Australian dollar, which has been sold against the NZ dollar this week, regained some ground on the day, ending at ended at NZ$1.1262/77 from an early NZ$1.1242/60 and a Wednesday finish of NZ$1.1266/81.
However, it remains well below Tuesday's NZ$1.1376/90 close.
The NZ dollar has benefitted from its high yield status, taking some of the samurai business from Australia as perceptions of falling local rates grow.
Most economists believe that another Australian interest rate cut is likely this year, following a 0.5 percentage point reduction in rates to 7.0 percent on July 31.
Westpac Bank economists saw a 75 percent chance rates would be cut by the end of the year. Such a move would occur around the same time the U.S. is expected to be raising rates.

"The prospective 100 basis point narrowing in the nominal short Australia-U.S. spread will be a negative for the currency," Westpac's senior International economist Helen Camp said in the bank's September currency review.
However, the samurai-related demand should not dry up completely, she said.
"The more limited Australia-Japan spread narrowing should continue to produce steady Japanese retail interest," she said.
The samurai related buying, and a recovering U.S. dollar, bouyed the Australian dollar against the yen, after earlier it had hovered above 86 yen through the morning.
In late trade, the Australian dollar was at 86.33/43 yen from from an early 86.05/15 and 86.80/90 late on Wednesday.
In trade weighted terms, the Australian dollar recovered from some morning weakness to close at 58.0, down from Wednesday's closing 58.2, but up on the midday reading of 57.9.
